text: This lab puts the last four lessons together into one program: you'll write an operation that allocates two qubits instead of one, entangles them instead of just superposing one, and reasons about outcomes that are correlated instead of independent.

You already know every ingredient. use with a tuple allocates both qubits in one statement, each starting in |0>. H on the first qubit puts just that one into superposition, same as before. The new piece is CNOT, the two-qubit controlled-not gate, which flips the target qubit if and only if the control qubit is One — and because the control is in superposition rather than a definite value, this is exactly where entanglement comes from.

Here's the full operation: allocate q0 and q1, apply H to q0 only, apply CNOT with q0 as control and q1 as target, measure both, and reset both. That single CNOT line is the entire new ingredient over everything from the last four lessons.

Tracing the exact amplitudes: starting state |00> is the vector one, zero, zero, zero. H on the first qubit turns this into an equal superposition of |00> and |10>. CNOT then swaps the |10> and |11> amplitude slots, because it flips the second qubit exactly when the first is one — and since nothing was on |11> or |01> to begin with, you land on amplitude only on |00> and |11>. Squaring those gives exactly zero point five and zero point five, and exactly zero on the other two outcomes. This is the Bell state — two outcomes possible, each at precisely fifty percent, and the other two genuinely impossible, not just unlikely.

Run CreateBellPair many times and tally the pairs you get back. You should see roughly half landing on Zero-Zero, roughly half on One-One, and effectively none on Zero-One or One-Zero. That's the part worth actually checking, not assuming. If you see a meaningful number of mismatched pairs, that's a bug in the circuit — applying H to the wrong qubit, or getting the control and target order backwards in CNOT — not a feature of entanglement.
That closes out Chapter 1's language fundamentals. Chapter 2 goes deeper on exactly what you allocated here: qubits and allocation patterns in Q#, starting with lesson 6.
